category: VSM simulation, graphs, instruments & microcontroller co-simulation
description: Proteus VSM: interactive and graph-based mixed-mode SPICE simulation, the generator and probe objects that stimulate and observe a circuit, the virtual instruments, microcontroller co-simulation with real firmware, the VSM Studio IDE and flowchart tools, and the SDK for writing custom simulator models.

tools.name: Interactive simulation (Play / Pause / Step / Stop)
tools.description: The animated real-time simulation mode. The transport controls at the bottom left run, pause, single-step and stop the simulation; while it runs, LEDs light, displays update, switches respond to clicks and — with the animation options enabled — wires are coloured by voltage and arrows show current direction. It is how a design is explored before any measurement is taken.
tools.usage: Debug > Run Simulation (F12) / Pause (Pause key) / Step (F11) / Stop (Shift+Break); or the Play/Pause/Step/Stop buttons at the bottom left
tools.example: Press F12; click the virtual push-button on the schematic and watch the LED and the LCD react in real time.
tools.notes: Interactive simulation runs as close to real time as the machine allows; use graph-based analysis when exact timing or measurement matters.

tools.name: Graph Mode and graph-based simulation
tools.description: Places an analysis graph on the schematic. Each graph object defines one analysis — its type, its time or frequency range and its options — and the probes and generators dragged onto it define what is plotted. Running the graph (space bar on the selected graph, or Graph > Simulate Graph) performs a precise, repeatable analysis independent of real-time animation.
tools.usage: Graph Mode on the left toolbar > pick the graph type in the object selector > drag out the graph rectangle on the sheet; drag probes onto it; press the space bar to simulate
tools.example: Graph Mode > ANALOGUE > drag a graph, drag the OUT voltage probe onto its left axis, double-click the graph to set Stop Time 20 ms, press space to run.
tools.notes: Graphs are part of the schematic and are saved with it, so an analysis set up once is repeatable by anyone who opens the design.

tools.name: Analogue (transient) graph
tools.description: Time-domain analysis of the analogue circuit — the equivalent of a SPICE .TRAN run. The graph's properties set the start and stop time and the maximum timestep, and the traces come from voltage and current probes dragged onto its axes. It is the workhorse graph for power supplies, oscillators, filters and any waveform question.
tools.usage: Graph Mode > ANALOGUE; double-click the graph for Start/Stop Time and options

parameters.name: Left / Right Axis Label and range
parameters.description: Two independent Y axes so voltage and current can share a graph.

parameters.name: Initial DC solution
parameters.description: Whether the run starts from the computed operating point.

tools.example: ANALOGUE graph, Stop Time 20m, drag probes V(OUT) and I(L1) onto the left and right axes, simulate.

tools.name: Digital graph
tools.description: Time-domain analysis of digital signals, drawn as logic-level traces and buses rather than analogue waveforms. Digital probes and bus probes are dragged onto it, and the result shows transitions, bus values and any contention or undefined states with the event-driven simulator's exact timing.
tools.usage: Graph Mode > DIGITAL; drag digital probes or a bus probe onto the graph
tools.example: DIGITAL graph over 10 ms, drag the SCL, SDA and the D[0..7] bus probes onto it to see the I2C transaction and the parallel bus side by side.

tools.name: Mixed graph
tools.description: Shows analogue and digital traces on one time axis, which is the point of a mixed-mode simulator: an ADC input waveform and the resulting digital code, or a PWM gate drive against the switching node voltage, are read off a single graph with a shared cursor.
tools.usage: Graph Mode > MIXED; drag both analogue and digital probes onto the graph
tools.example: MIXED graph, drag the sensor voltage probe and the SPI clock/data digital probes on together to correlate the conversion with the bus traffic.

tools.name: Frequency graph
tools.description: AC small-signal analysis: the circuit is linearised about its operating point and swept over frequency, producing magnitude and phase (Bode) plots. The graph's properties set the start and stop frequency, the interval (decades/octaves/linear) and the number of steps, and a reference generator supplies the AC stimulus.
tools.usage: Graph Mode > FREQUENCY; set Start/Stop Frequency, Interval and Number of Steps; assign the reference generator
tools.example: FREQUENCY graph 10 Hz to 1 MHz, 10 steps per decade, reference generator V1, probe on the filter output — magnitude on the left axis, phase on the right.

tools.name: DC Transfer Curve graph (DC Sweep)
tools.description: Sweeps a source over a range and plots a DC output against it, producing transfer characteristics — a potential divider's linearity, a transistor's transfer curve, a comparator's threshold. A second nested sweep produces a family of curves.
tools.usage: Graph Mode > DC SWEEP; set the sweep source, its start/stop values and the number of steps
tools.example: DC SWEEP of V1 from 0 to 5 V in 100 steps, probe on the divider output, to confirm the transfer ratio across the range.

tools.name: AC / DC Parameter Sweep graphs
tools.description: Repeat a frequency or DC analysis while stepping a component value or a named property, producing a family of curves that shows sensitivity to tolerance, load or a tuning element. The swept property is nominated in the graph's properties, which is how a compensation network or a filter is tuned on screen.
tools.usage: Graph Mode > AC SWEEP / DC SWEEP with a swept component property; set the component, property, start/stop and step count
tools.example: AC SWEEP graph sweeping R2 from 1k to 100k in 5 steps, probe on the output, to see how the feedback resistor moves the corner frequency.

tools.name: Noise graph
tools.description: Computes the output noise spectral density and the equivalent input noise over a frequency range, with a per-component contribution breakdown in the simulation log. It is how a low-noise amplifier or a sensor front end is evaluated before it is built.
tools.usage: Graph Mode > NOISE; set the frequency range and the reference (input) generator
tools.example: NOISE graph 10 Hz to 100 kHz with the input generator as reference; read the total output noise and the dominant contributor from the log.
tools.notes: Part of the Advanced Simulation Features; the base simulation licence does not include the noise, distortion and conformance graphs.

tools.name: Distortion graph
tools.description: Measures harmonic and intermodulation distortion of an analogue stage by driving it with one or two tones and analysing the output spectrum. Used for audio and instrumentation circuits where linearity, not just gain, is the specification.
tools.usage: Graph Mode > DISTORTION; set the analysis frequency range and the reference generator(s)
tools.example: DISTORTION graph on the audio output stage to read second- and third-harmonic levels across the audio band.
tools.notes: Part of the Advanced Simulation Features option.

tools.name: Fourier graph
tools.description: Transforms a transient result into the frequency domain, showing the harmonic content of a waveform — switching harmonics on a supply node, the spectrum of a PWM output, the purity of an oscillator. The transform window is set by the underlying transient range and resolution.
tools.usage: Graph Mode > FOURIER; set the transient window and the frequency range to display
tools.example: FOURIER graph over a 20 ms window of the class-D output, displayed from 0 to 100 kHz.

tools.name: Audio graph
tools.description: Runs a transient analysis and renders the result as audio, so a probed node can be played through the PC's sound card or written to a WAV file. It is a Labcenter speciality for audio circuit work — the fastest way to hear whether a filter or distortion stage does what was intended.
tools.usage: Graph Mode > AUDIO; drag a probe onto the graph, set the time window, simulate and press play
tools.example: AUDIO graph over 2 s of the amplifier output driven by a WAV-file generator; play the result and compare it with the source file.

tools.name: Transfer / Impedance graphs
tools.description: Reports small-signal transfer characteristics: the DC transfer function between an input source and an output, and the input and output impedance of the circuit as a function of frequency. They answer 'what does this stage look like to its neighbours' without constructing a test bench.
tools.usage: Graph Mode > TRANSFER (and the input/output impedance options in the analysis properties)
tools.example: TRANSFER graph between V1 and the output node to read the gain, input resistance and output resistance in one run.

tools.name: Interactive graph
tools.description: A graph that records data while an interactive simulation is running, so a waveform can be captured from a session in which the user clicks buttons and turns virtual pots. It bridges the animated and the measured worlds: you drive the circuit by hand and still get a plotted, measurable trace.
tools.usage: Graph Mode > INTERACTIVE; drag probes onto it and run the simulation with F12
tools.example: INTERACTIVE graph on the motor current probe; run the simulation, press the virtual start button, and the inrush current is captured on the graph.

tools.name: Conformance graph / Conformance Analysis
tools.description: Software quality assurance for embedded designs: a conformance graph records a reference trace of the system's behaviour and later runs are compared against it automatically, so a firmware change that alters timing or protocol behaviour is flagged as a regression rather than being spotted by eye.
tools.usage: Graph Mode > CONFORMANCE; capture a reference, then re-run after each firmware change
tools.example: Capture a conformance reference of the I2C transaction, change the driver code, re-run — differences in the bus timing are reported as non-conformance.
tools.notes: Part of the Advanced Simulation Features option.

tools.name: Generator Mode
tools.description: Places a signal source on a net. The analogue generators are DC, SINE, PULSE, EXP, SFFM, PWLIN, FILE (a data file of time/value pairs) and AUDIO (a WAV file); the digital generators are DSTATE (fixed level), DEDGE (single transition), DPULSE (single pulse), DCLOCK (continuous clock) and DPATTERN (an arbitrary bit sequence). A generator can be a current source instead of a voltage source, and is the reference for frequency, noise and distortion analyses.
tools.usage: Generator Mode on the left toolbar > pick the generator type in the object selector > click on the wire; double-click to edit its parameters

parameters.name: SINE
parameters.description: Offset, amplitude, frequency, time delay, damping factor and phase.

parameters.name: PULSE
parameters.description: Initial and pulsed value, delay, rise and fall time, pulse width and period.

parameters.name: PWLIN
parameters.description: Arbitrary piecewise-linear list of time/value points.

parameters.name: DCLOCK
parameters.description: Digital clock with period/frequency, first-edge time and pulse width.

parameters.name: DPATTERN
parameters.description: Arbitrary digital sequence with a bit string, timing and optional looping.

parameters.name: Current Source / Isolate Before
parameters.description: Makes the generator a current source, or isolates the node from what drives it.

tools.example: Generator Mode > SINE > click the input net > Amplitude 1 V, Frequency 1 kHz; the same generator also supplies the AC reference for a FREQUENCY graph.

tools.name: Voltage and Current Probes
tools.description: The measurement objects. A voltage probe attaches to a wire and reports its node voltage; a current probe is placed in series in a wire and reports the current through it with a direction arrow. During interactive simulation a probe displays its live value on the schematic; dragged onto a graph it becomes a plotted trace.
tools.usage: Probe Mode on the left toolbar > choose VOLTAGE or CURRENT > click the wire; drag the probe onto a graph to plot it
tools.example: Place a voltage probe named OUT on the filter output and a current probe in the inductor's wire, then drag both onto an ANALOGUE graph.
tools.notes: Current probes must be placed in a wire segment, not on a junction; the arrow shows the assumed positive direction.

tools.name: Tape recorder
tools.description: Records the signals on a set of nets during one simulation and plays them back into another part of the design (or another design) in a later run. It lets a large system be simulated in stages — capture the stimulus a subsystem sees, then simulate that subsystem alone at full resolution.
tools.usage: Place a TAPE object from the object selector, wire it to the nets to record, run once to record, then switch it to playback
tools.example: Record the ADC input and control signals during the full-system run, then replay them into the isolated analogue front end for a fine-timestep analysis.

tools.name: Oscilloscope (virtual instrument)
tools.description: A four-channel virtual oscilloscope with per-channel gain and position, AC/DC coupling, timebase, trigger source, level and edge, and cursors. It is wired into the schematic like a real scope and displays live during interactive simulation, which makes it the natural instrument for exploratory work.
tools.usage: Virtual Instruments Mode > OSCILLOSCOPE > place and wire channels A-D; run the simulation to open its front panel
tools.example: Wire channel A to the gate drive and B to the switching node, set the timebase to 2 µs/div and trigger on A rising, then run.

tools.name: Logic Analyser (virtual instrument)
tools.description: Captures many digital channels and buses at high resolution with a configurable trigger and capture depth, then displays them with cursors and measurement readouts. It is the tool for debugging bus timing and protocol behaviour that a scope cannot show across enough channels.
tools.usage: Virtual Instruments Mode > LOGIC ANALYSER > wire the channels and bus inputs; set resolution and trigger on its front panel
tools.example: Wire the address and data buses to the analyser's bus inputs, trigger on the chip-select falling edge, and read the bus cycle timing off the cursors.

tools.name: Virtual Terminal
tools.description: A serial terminal attached to a UART's TX and RX pins. It displays what the firmware prints and lets typed characters be sent back into the simulation, with configurable baud rate, data bits, parity, stop bits and send/receive echo. It is the standard way to interact with and debug embedded firmware in Proteus.
tools.usage: Virtual Instruments Mode > VIRTUAL TERMINAL > wire RXD/TXD to the MCU's UART pins; set the baud rate in its properties

parameters.name: Baud Rate / Data Bits / Parity / Stop Bits
parameters.description: Must match the firmware's UART configuration exactly or the output is garbage.

parameters.name: RX/TX Polarity
parameters.description: Normal or inverted, for direct connection versus through a transceiver.

tools.example: Wire the terminal to RC6/RC7, set 9600 8N1, run — the firmware's printf output appears in the terminal window.

tools.name: SPI Debugger and I2C Debugger
tools.description: Protocol analysers that sit on a bus and decode the traffic into readable transactions, and can also inject data onto the bus as a master or slave. They turn 'the sensor is not responding' into a visible sequence of addresses, acknowledges and data bytes.
tools.usage: Virtual Instruments Mode > SPI DEBUGGER / I2C DEBUGGER > wire to the bus lines; open its window during simulation
tools.example: Place the I2C Debugger across SDA/SCL and run — the window lists each START, address, ACK/NAK and data byte of the sensor transaction.

tools.name: Signal Generator and Pattern Generator (virtual instruments)
tools.description: Interactive stimulus instruments with real front panels: the Signal Generator produces sine, square, triangle and sawtooth waveforms with adjustable frequency, amplitude and offset plus AM/FM modulation inputs; the Pattern Generator produces a programmable digital sequence with clock, trigger and hold controls. Unlike generator objects, their controls can be turned while the simulation runs.
tools.usage: Virtual Instruments Mode > SIGNAL GENERATOR / PATTERN GENERATOR; adjust the front-panel controls during the run
tools.example: Wire the Signal Generator to the amplifier input, run, and sweep the frequency knob by hand to find the passband by ear and eye.

tools.name: Voltmeters, Ammeters, Counter/Timer and Wattmeter
tools.description: Live numeric instruments placed on the schematic: DC and AC voltmeters and ammeters (with selectable range), the Counter/Timer in frequency, period, time-interval or event-count mode, and the wattmeter which measures power from a voltage and current pair. They display their reading directly on the sheet during interactive simulation.
tools.usage: Virtual Instruments Mode > DC VOLTMETER / AC VOLTMETER / DC AMMETER / AC AMMETER / COUNTER TIMER / WATTMETER
tools.example: Place a DC ammeter in the supply lead and a DC voltmeter across the load; run and read the quiescent current and rail voltage straight off the schematic.

tools.name: System Meter
tools.description: A live probing instrument introduced in Proteus 9.2 that displays measured values from the running simulation in a consolidated panel, so several quantities can be watched at once without covering the schematic in individual meters.
tools.usage: Virtual Instruments Mode > System Meter (Proteus 9.2 and later); add the signals to watch
tools.example: Add the rail voltage, load current and MCU clock to the System Meter and watch them together while stepping through the firmware.

tools.name: Microcontroller simulation (Program File property)
tools.description: The core of VSM: a microcontroller part on the schematic is given a compiled firmware image through its Program File property and the simulator executes that machine code instruction by instruction, modelling the on-chip peripherals (ports, timers, ADC, USART, SPI, I2C, PWM, interrupts) down to pin waveforms. Supported families include PIC, AVR, 8051, ARM Cortex-M, MSP430, Arduino and Raspberry Pi Pico.
tools.usage: Double-click the MCU > Program File = <.hex/.cof/.elf>; set Processor Clock Frequency and the configuration word/fuses in Advanced Properties

parameters.name: Program File
parameters.description: HEX (no symbols), COF or ELF/DWARF (with symbols, enabling source-level debugging).

parameters.name: Processor Clock Frequency
parameters.description: Simulated clock; it must match what the firmware assumes for timing to be right.

parameters.name: Configuration words / fuses
parameters.description: Oscillator selection, watchdog, brown-out and other device options, set in the part's advanced properties.

tools.example: PIC16F877A > Program File = build\blink.cof, Processor Clock Frequency = 8MHz, Advanced Properties > Oscillator = HS; run and single-step the C source.
tools.notes: Use a COF or ELF image rather than a plain HEX whenever you want breakpoints, variable watches and source stepping.

tools.name: Source Code tab / VSM Studio
tools.description: The integrated firmware IDE. It holds the firmware project alongside the schematic, calls an external compiler toolchain (MPLAB XC8/XC16/XC32, AVR-GCC, the Arduino AVR core, Keil, GCC for ARM), and then debugs the built image inside the running simulation. System > Compilers Configuration is where toolchains are located or downloaded.
tools.usage: Source Code tab; Project > Add/New Firmware Project; System > Compilers Configuration; Build then Debug > Run
tools.example: Source > New Firmware Project > controller ATmega328P, compiler Arduino AVR > write the sketch > Build > F12 to simulate with the real hardware around it.

tools.name: Breakpoints, single stepping and source debugging
tools.description: Full source-level debugging of the simulated firmware: breakpoints set in the source or disassembly, step into/over/out, run to cursor, and a halt that freezes the entire circuit so pin states, peripheral registers and analogue node voltages can be inspected at that exact instruction.
tools.usage: Click the gutter to toggle a breakpoint; Debug > Step Into (F11) / Step Over (F10) / Step Out / Run To Cursor; the transport controls also step
tools.example: Set a breakpoint in the ADC interrupt handler, press F12 — the simulation halts with the input waveform frozen mid-conversion so the register values can be read.

tools.name: Debug windows (variables, watch, registers, memory)
tools.description: The inspection windows available while the simulation is halted or running: local and global variable views, a Watch window with user-chosen expressions that can update live, CPU register views, program and data memory dumps, the stack and the disassembly. They are opened from the Debug menu once a simulation is running.
tools.usage: Debug menu > (Watch Window, Variables, Registers, Program Memory, Data Memory, Call Stack, Disassembly) — populated once the simulation is started
tools.example: Debug > Watch Window > add `adc_result` and set it to update in real time so the variable is graphed against the analogue input as the simulation runs.

tools.name: Remote debugging with an external IDE
tools.description: Proteus can serve as the debug target for Microchip MPLAB X, Atmel/Microchip Studio, Keil uVision and STM32CubeIDE (over GDB). The firmware is built and debugged in the vendor IDE while the simulated circuit responds in Proteus, which suits teams whose build system is already established outside Proteus.
tools.usage: Debug > Enable Remote Debug Monitor in Proteus, then select the Proteus VSM debug tool/connection in the external IDE
tools.example:
1. Proteus: Debug > Enable Remote Debug Monitor.
2. MPLAB X: choose the Proteus VSM hardware tool for the project.
3. Start debugging — breakpoints hit in MPLAB while the LEDs change in Proteus.

tools.name: Visual Designer (flowchart programming)
tools.description: Graphical firmware development for Arduino, Raspberry Pi and MicroPython targets: the program is built as a flowchart of statements, peripheral method calls, loops and decisions over a selected hardware shield set, compiled automatically and simulated on the schematic. It removes the toolchain setup step entirely for education and rapid prototyping.
tools.usage: File > New Project > tick 'Create Firmware Project' > Visual Designer for Arduino / Raspberry Pi; build in the Visual Designer tab
tools.example: New Visual Designer Arduino project with a Grove shield, drag a LOOP block containing 'LED write HIGH', 'DELAY 500', 'LED write LOW', 'DELAY 500', then Build and Run.

tools.name: IoT Builder
tools.description: Extends Visual Designer with a drag-and-drop dashboard for phone or browser front ends and MQTT connectivity, so an internet-connected appliance and its control app are designed, simulated and deployed together from Proteus. Multi-appliance systems are built by linking several devices through the broker.
tools.usage: New project with IoT Builder for Arduino / Raspberry Pi / MicroPython; design the dashboard alongside the flowchart
tools.example: Build a thermostat flowchart, add a dashboard gauge and setpoint slider bound to MQTT topics, simulate the whole loop before deploying to real hardware.

tools.name: Peripheral models (LCDs, LEDs, motors, sensors, displays)
tools.description: Proteus ships animated models of the peripherals an embedded design actually uses: character and graphic LCDs, seven-segment and dot-matrix displays, keypads, DC, stepper and servo motors, relays, temperature and pressure sensors, real-time clocks, EEPROMs, SD cards, USB and Ethernet devices, and (in recent releases) BLE and RFID models. They respond to the simulated firmware exactly as the real part would.
tools.usage: Pick them from the library like any component (Component Mode > P) and wire them to the microcontroller
tools.example: Place an LM016L character LCD, wire it to the MCU's port, and watch the firmware's text appear on the simulated display.

tools.name: Simulation Advisor
tools.description: Labcenter's diagnostic helper: it takes a message from the simulation log and links it to an explanation of the cause and the usual remedies — missing models, unconnected power, singular matrices, timestep failures, missing program files. It is the first stop when a simulation refuses to start.
tools.usage: Reached from the simulation log entries, or Help > Simulation Advisor
tools.example: Log reports 'Singular matrix' — the Advisor explains the floating-node and zero-resistance-loop causes and how to add a small series or shunt resistance.

tools.name: Convergence troubleshooting
tools.description: The standard remedies when a Proteus simulation fails to converge or reports a singular matrix or timestep failure: give every node a DC path to ground, avoid ideal zero-resistance loops and ideal voltage sources in parallel, add small series resistance and realistic parasitics, give switching elements finite rise and fall times, reduce the maximum timestep, and relax the tolerances on System > Set Simulation Options as a last resort.
tools.usage: System > Set Simulation Options (tolerances, timestep and iteration limits); redesign the offending node as indicated by the log
tools.example:
1. Read the simulation log for the offending node.
2. Add a 1 mΩ series resistance in the ideal source loop.
3. Reduce the maximum timestep, and only then relax the tolerance settings.
tools.notes: Relaxing tolerances can turn a failure into a converged wrong answer; tighten them again once the circuit runs.

tools.name: VSM SDK: writing a custom model
tools.description: The documented extension route for the simulator. A custom model is a C++ DLL that includes Labcenter's vsm.hpp and exports the create/delete entry points for its model class — `createspicemodel`/`deletespicemodel`, `createdsimmodel`/`deletedsimmodel`, `createmixedmodel`/`deletemixedmodel` or `createactivemodel`/`deleteactivemodel` — each taking the device name and an ILICENCESERVER pointer. The class implements the matching interface and receives an IINSTANCE giving access to the placed component's pins and properties.
tools.usage: Build a DLL against vsm.hpp exporting the create/delete pair for the model kind; reference it from the part through its MODFILE/model property
tools.notes: Four model kinds exist — SPICE (analogue), DSIM (digital), mixed and active (animated). Pick the one matching the behaviour you need; an active model is what gives a component interactive graphics.

tools.name: VSM SDK: IINSTANCE, pins and callbacks
tools.description: Inside a custom model, `IINSTANCE` represents the placed component and gives access to its schematic properties and its pins; pin objects expose the current logic state and methods to drive a new state at a given time; and `IDSIMCKT::setcallback` schedules a call to the model's `callback(ABSTIME time, EVENTID eventid)` at a future simulation time, which is how clocks, timers and delayed outputs are implemented.
tools.usage: VOID setup(IINSTANCE* instance, IDSIMCKT* ckt); VOID simulate(ABSTIME time, DSIMMODES mode); VOID callback(ABSTIME time, EVENTID eventid);

tools.name: SPICE model attachment (SPICEMODEL / SPICEFILE)
tools.description: The no-code way to give a part a vendor simulation model: add a SPICEMODEL property naming the .MODEL or .SUBCKT and a SPICEFILE property naming the file that contains it, in the component's Other Properties. Proteus then resolves the model when the netlist is built, and the simulation log reports whether it was found and how the pins were mapped.
tools.usage:
Component properties > Other Properties:
SPICEMODEL=<model or subcircuit name>
SPICEFILE=<path to .lib/.mod file>
tools.example:
SPICEMODEL=OPA2277
SPICEFILE=models\opa2277.lib
tools.notes: Pin order must match the subcircuit's declared node order; check the model file's header comment and verify the operating point before trusting the results.

tools.name: Advanced Simulation Features (ASF)
tools.description: The licensed option that adds the analysis graphs beyond the basic set — frequency, noise, distortion, Fourier, parameter sweeps, conformance analysis — together with performance measurement and tolerance handling. Without it, Proteus still simulates interactively and with analogue, digital and mixed transient graphs, but the analytical measurement graphs are unavailable.
tools.usage: Licensed option; the additional graph types appear in the Graph Mode object selector when it is enabled
tools.example: With ASF enabled, add a NOISE graph and a DISTORTION graph to the audio stage to quantify what interactive simulation only suggests.

tools.name: Graph measurement cursors and data export
tools.description: Once a graph has been simulated it can be maximised into its own window, where cursors read exact X/Y values and differences, traces can be added, removed and rescaled, and the underlying data exported to a data file for analysis elsewhere. Log/linear axes and multiple Y axes make wide-dynamic-range results readable.
tools.usage: Click a graph and press the space bar to simulate, then double-click (or Graph > Maximise) to open its window; use the cursors and the Graph > Export Graph Data command
tools.example: Maximise the FREQUENCY graph, drop a cursor at the -3 dB point to read the corner frequency, then export the trace data to CSV.
